source: Book: Project Management Next Generation (Kerzner, Zeitoun & Vargas, 2022) — Pillar 8: Adaptive Frameworks and Life Cycles (project closure and benefits harvesting)
question: A hybrid project has rolled out a new warehouse-management system to 14 distribution centers, and the final site accepted the deliverables last week. Functional managers want all nine team members back immediately. The operations director, who owns the productivity benefit, worries that without expert help her supervisors will slip back to old spreadsheets before the new ways of working stick. The benefits plan expects gains to build over the next five months. What should the project manager do?
options: Release all team members as the functional managers request, and give the operations director a list of experts she can call
Keep the full team together until the productivity gains appear, since the project has not succeeded until its benefits are real
Agree with the sponsor and operations director on a small, time-boxed support role for key experts, then close and release the rest
Ask the operations director to hire contractors for adoption support, since the project's duties ended when deliverables were accepted
hint: Benefits need time and support to be harvested; what is the smallest arrangement that protects them without keeping the project open indefinitely?
why: Kerzner notes that for strategic projects some team members may need to stay involved after delivery to help stakeholders extract the benefits, while ownership of harvesting sits with the business. A small, time-boxed arrangement for key experts — agreed with the sponsor, the operations director as benefit owner, and the functional managers — protects adoption during the critical months. The rest of the team can be released and the project formally closed, keeping accountability clear.
how: When benefits depend on adoption after delivery, negotiate a limited, time-boxed support arrangement under the benefit owner, then complete formal closure and release the remaining resources.
optionNotes: Incorrect — An on-call list is weak support for a known adoption risk; relapse to old tools could erode the benefit that justified the project.
Incorrect — Keeping all nine people for five months is costly and unnecessary; the business, not the whole project team, harvests the benefits.
Correct — A targeted, time-boxed support role under the benefit owner protects adoption while the project closes and releases most people.
Incorrect — Declaring the job done at acceptance ignores the transition and knowledge-transfer duties of closure and adds avoidable cost.
deepDive: Kerzner describes a benefits-harvesting period after strategic projects deliver their outcomes: the business value gap closes gradually, and someone must own the harvesting, which may or may not include people who built the deliverables. Harvesting can take months or years and may need readjustment. In PMI terms this touches knowledge transfer, organizational change and transition planning, and the sponsor stays accountable for benefits after closure. Exam trap: 'the project ends at acceptance' and 'the project continues until benefits are realized' are both extremes; a tailored middle path is usually best.

source: Book: Project Management Next Generation (Kerzner, Zeitoun & Vargas, 2022) — Pillar 10: Value-Driven and Business-Related Metrics (learning from successful projects too)
question: A 14-month network-modernization project finished three weeks early and under budget, and the customer is delighted. As closure begins, the sponsor tells the project manager to skip the lessons-learned session: 'Nothing went wrong, so there is nothing to learn — let the team move on.' Several team members believe their new vendor-coordination approach was the main reason for the early finish. What should the project manager do?
options: Skip the session as the sponsor asks, since lessons-learned reviews exist mainly to stop mistakes from being repeated
Hold a short, focused session to capture what made the project succeed and share it in the organization's repository
Ask the team members to email their thoughts on the vendor approach to the PMO after they start their next assignments
Delay closure until a full independent audit of the project is complete so that the success factors can be formally validated
hint: Is a lessons-learned review only about what went wrong?
why: Lessons learned and best practices come from successes as well as failures, and the vendor-coordination approach is a candidate best practice other projects could reuse. A short, focused session before the team disperses captures it while memories are fresh, respects the sponsor's concern about time, and stores the knowledge where future projects can find it. The project manager can explain that value to the sponsor rather than simply dropping the activity.
how: At closure, always capture lessons — including success factors — before the team disbands, scale the effort to the project, and store them in the organization's knowledge repository for reuse.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Lessons-learned reviews also capture repeatable success factors; skipping one throws away a practice that shortened the schedule.
Correct — A brief, focused session preserves the success factors while the team is together and makes them available to future projects.
Incorrect — Asking for input after people have moved on yields sparse, unstructured feedback and usually loses the most useful details.
Incorrect — A full audit is out of proportion for capturing a good practice, and it delays closure without adding much learning value.
deepDive: Kerzner stresses that lessons and best practices can be found in projects heading for success as well as in troubled ones, and that a close look at an apparently successful project sometimes reveals hidden problems. He also lists the lack of a process for capturing lessons and best practices as a cause of repeated failure. PMBOK treats lessons learned as an ongoing activity — captured throughout, consolidated at closure and transferred to organizational process assets. In agile teams, retrospectives serve the same purpose continuously.

source: Book: Project Management Next Generation (Kerzner, Zeitoun & Vargas, 2022) — Pillar 8: Adaptive Frameworks and Life Cycles (project closure: administrative closure)
question: The customer formally accepted the final deliverable of a factory-automation project two weeks ago. While reconciling costs, the project manager notices that several engineers are still booking time to the project's charge code for 'tidying up files', and a purchase order for spare sensors that were never needed remains open. Finance wants to publish the final cost report next week. What should the project manager do?
options: Complete the remaining closure tasks, close the charge code and the unneeded purchase order, then reconcile the final costs
Leave the charge code open for another month so that the engineers can finish any clean-up work they might need to do later
Ask finance to publish the cost report now and treat any further hours and purchase orders as normal operating expenses
Move the open purchase order and the engineers' hours to a new project so that the final report for this project looks clean
hint: What has to be true of the project's accounts before a final cost figure can be trusted?
why: Once deliverables are accepted, administrative closure means finishing any genuinely required closure tasks and then closing the accounts so no further costs are charged: closing charge codes, closing or cancelling unneeded purchase orders under their terms, and reconciling actual costs for the final report. This gives finance an accurate final cost and stops open-ended spending on a completed project.
how: For financial closure: finish required closure tasks, close charge codes and open purchase orders, reconcile costs against the budget, then publish the final report and archive the records.
optionNotes: Correct — Finishing the closure tasks, then closing accounts and open orders, stops cost leakage and produces an accurate, reconciled final cost.
Incorrect — An open charge code invites unplanned spending on a finished project and delays the accurate final cost that finance needs.
Incorrect — Publishing before reconciling yields an inaccurate report and hides project costs in operations, distorting both budgets.
Incorrect — Shifting costs to another project to make a report look clean misrepresents actual costs and breaches the PMI Code's honesty standard.
deepDive: Kerzner notes that on traditional projects closure happens once the deliverables are accepted: the team performs administrative and contractual closure and moves on. Administrative closure covers financial closure (charge codes, invoices, cost reconciliation), archiving records, final reports and releasing resources; contractual closure covers verifying that contract terms were met, settling claims and formally closing procurements. One common exam trap is to 'leave things open just in case'; another is to disguise costs, which is an ethics issue rather than an accounting shortcut.

source: Book: Project Management Next Generation (Kerzner, Zeitoun & Vargas, 2022) — Pillar 4: Digitalization (information warehouses and knowledge repositories)
question: A program of six agile teams is closing after two years of building a public-transport ticketing platform. Each team kept its retrospective notes in its own wiki space, and a new program starting next month will reuse the same payment technology. The new program's lead says she has no idea where to find what these teams learned. As the closing program's delivery lead, what should you do?
options: Tell the new program lead which team wikis exist so that she can search the retrospective notes whenever she needs something
Archive all six team wikis in a read-only folder so that the program's records are complete and protected after closure
Ask each team to email its most important lessons directly to the new program lead before the teams are released next week
Curate the key lessons into the organization's searchable repository and walk the new program team through them
hint: Knowledge that exists but cannot be found or understood has not really been transferred; what would make it usable by the next team?
why: Kerzner treats knowledge repositories as a core digital asset: learning is valuable only if others can find and apply it. Consolidating the recurring themes from six teams' retrospectives into the organizational repository, tagged so they are searchable, turns scattered notes into reusable knowledge, and a short walkthrough with the new team passes on tacit context that documents miss. It is also a natural closure activity for the program.
how: At closure, lift lessons from local team spaces into the organization's knowledge repository in a curated, searchable form, and pair documents with conversations so tacit knowledge transfers too.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Pointing to six raw wikis leaves the new team to dig through scattered notes, so relevant lessons are likely to be missed.
Incorrect — A read-only archive preserves the records but does nothing to make the lessons findable or usable by the next program.
Incorrect — Ad-hoc emails to one person are unstructured, easily lost and unavailable to anyone else who needs the knowledge later.
Correct — A curated, searchable repository entry plus a walkthrough makes the lessons findable, reusable and understood by the next team.
deepDive: Kerzner's digitalization pillar describes information warehouses and knowledge repositories that store lessons learned, best practices and project data for reuse, feeding business intelligence and better decisions. PMBOK distinguishes explicit knowledge, which can be codified in repositories, from tacit knowledge, which transfers best through conversation, mentoring and communities of practice, so good transfer uses both. In agile programs, retrospective insights tend to stay local to one team; closure is the moment to lift cross-team lessons to the organization. Exam trap: archiving is about records retention, not knowledge transfer.

topic: Releasing an agile team at close
source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 10 · Agile practice
question: An agile team has delivered the final release of a mobile-banking feature, and the product owner has confirmed that the remaining backlog items are not worth funding. The team will be disbanded at the end of the month and its members reassigned to other products, and an operations support group will run the feature from now on. Which actions should the project manager prioritize before the team is released? (Select two.)
options: Hold a final retrospective covering the whole project and share the key insights with other teams in the organization
Run one more sprint to finish the lowest-priority backlog items so that the backlog is empty when the team disbands
Transfer knowledge to the support group through documentation, pairing sessions and a clear handover of open issues
Ask the functional managers to write performance reviews once team members have already moved to their new roles
Keep the product backlog active and continue refining items in case funding is approved again in the coming months
hint: The product owner has already decided what not to build; what must still happen so that learning and operational knowledge outlast the team?
why: The product owner has decided the remaining backlog is not worth funding, so the focus shifts to preserving learning and enabling operations. A final whole-project retrospective captures insights for the wider organization, and structured knowledge transfer to the support group — documentation, pairing and an open-issue handover — lets the feature be run safely. Both must happen while the team still exists.
how: Closing an agile project: respect the product owner's value decision on remaining scope, run a final retrospective, transfer knowledge to whoever will operate the product, recognize the team, then release people.
optionNotes: Correct — A whole-project retrospective captures lessons while the team is still together and spreads them beyond this one team.
Incorrect — The product owner judged these items not worth funding; building them anyway spends money without matching value.
Correct — Structured knowledge transfer and a clean issue handover let the support group run the feature without the original team.
Incorrect — Performance input should be given while the project manager can still observe and discuss it, not after people have left.
Incorrect — Continuing to refine a backlog for an unfunded product consumes effort; archive it with the product owner instead.
deepDive: Agile projects often end when the product owner decides the remaining backlog no longer justifies its cost — delivering enough value, not every item, is the point. Closure activities still apply: a final retrospective, knowledge transfer to operations or a successor team, archiving the backlog and artifacts, recognizing contributions, giving performance input, and releasing people through their resource managers. Many organizations prefer to keep stable teams together and bring new work to them; when a team must disband, knowledge transfer matters even more. 'Finish every backlog item before closing' is a common exam distractor.

source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 10 · Retiring project environments, subscriptions and access at closure
question: An agile team of four employees and seven contract developers has finished a loyalty-rewards feature for a grocery chain's mobile app, and the product owner has accepted the final increment. The contracts end on Friday, and a two-person support team will maintain the app. During the project the team created six cloud test environments, bought a paid feature-flag service that now controls live promotions, and gave every contractor access to the code repository and to a copy of customer data. What should the project manager ensure as part of closing the project?
options: Leave every environment, service and access right in place for three months in case support needs the contractors
Review each environment, service and access right with the product owner, then transfer, retire or revoke it
Ask cloud operations to delete every environment and service the project created on Friday so that costs stop
Record the environments and access rights in the lessons learned so that the next team sets them up with more care
hint: Some of what the project created is still needed by the product and some is not — who can tell which is which?
why: Closure includes winding down the project's own arrangements, not just accepting the product. Leftover environments and subscriptions keep costing money, and contractors who keep repository and customer-data access after their contracts end are a security and privacy exposure. Yet the feature-flag service now runs live promotions, so blanket deletion would break the product. Reviewing each item with the product owner, transferring what the product still needs to the support team, and retiring or revoking the rest — including contractor access on their last day — closes the project cleanly and safely.
how: At closure, inventory everything the project created or granted — environments, licenses, subscriptions, accounts and data copies — and, with the product or operations owner, decide for each item whether to transfer, retire or revoke it.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Unused environments keep billing, and leaving former contractors with access to customer data is a serious security and privacy risk.
Correct — A joint review keeps what the product still needs under a named owner and removes the cost and access the project no longer needs.
Incorrect — Blanket deletion would switch off the feature-flag service that runs live promotions and could destroy data the support team needs.
Incorrect — Recording the issue for future teams does nothing about the costs and access risks that exist on this project today.
deepDive: Administrative closure covers more than documents and final acceptance: the project must release the resources it holds, and in digital work those include cloud environments, tool subscriptions, service accounts, licenses and copies of data. Items without an owner become orphaned infrastructure that keeps billing and is rarely patched. Access for people leaving the project, especially external contractors, should be revoked on their exit date in line with the organization's security policy. In agile product settings the product owner decides which tools and environments the product still needs, and the support or operations team takes them over formally.

source: Book: Project Management Next Generation (Kerzner, Zeitoun & Vargas, 2022) — Pillar 8: Adaptive Frameworks and Life Cycles (the wrong definition of success as a cause of failure)
question: A hybrid project installed self-service kiosks in 30 branches of a credit union, with the hardware rolled out on a fixed plan and the kiosk software built in sprints. It finished six weeks late and 9% over its original budget; the change log shows both variances came from two sponsor-approved changes, accessibility features and a second language, with the baselines updated each time. Early data show kiosk use 40% above the business-case forecast. The PMO's closure template rates success against the original baseline only, so the PMO lead says the project must be rated 'unsuccessful'. What should the project manager do?
options: Report results against the original and approved baselines, explain the changes, and add the early outcome data
Rate the project unsuccessful as the template requires, since the original baseline was the commitment at approval
Ask the sponsor to overrule the PMO lead and rate the project successful, since the sponsor owns the business case
Leave the rating blank until a full year of kiosk usage data is available, and close the project without a rating
hint: Which baseline reflects what the organization actually agreed to deliver, and what else shows whether the investment worked?
why: Performance is normally judged against the current approved baselines, which here include two changes the sponsor authorized through change control; measured that way, the project delivered what was agreed. Kerzner also warns that using the wrong definition of success, such as time and cost alone, is a cause of failure, and the early outcome data show the business case being exceeded. Reporting both baselines transparently, explaining the approved changes, and adding the outcome evidence gives governance an honest, complete picture, and the template gap can go into the lessons learned. Letting either the PMO lead or the sponsor impose a rating without that evidence, or skipping the rating, is less transparent.
how: At closure, evaluate the project against its approved, change-controlled baselines and its intended outcomes, show variances from the original plan with their causes, and feed any flaw in the closure template into lessons learned.
optionNotes: Correct — Shows the full, honest picture: the original commitment, the approved changes that altered it, and early evidence that value is being delivered.
Incorrect — Ignores changes the sponsor formally approved and judges success on time and cost alone, which misrepresents what the project delivered.
Incorrect — Using the sponsor's authority to impose a rating replaces evidence with influence and leaves the template's flaw unaddressed.
Incorrect — Closure should record an evaluation now; outcome measurement continues under the benefit owner and need not hold up the closure report.
deepDive: Among the book's causes of complete or partial failure are a heavy focus on deliverables rather than value and the use of the wrong definition of project success. Closure reports that compare only time, cost and scope with the original plan can make a project that absorbed valuable approved changes look like a failure, while one that hit its dates but produced no benefits looks like a success. PMI practice measures performance against the approved baselines, which change only through change control, and reports variance from the original plan separately as an estimating lesson. Good closure reports combine delivery performance with early outcome evidence and hand longer-term benefit measurement to the business owner.

topic: Settling a claim before contract closure
source: Book: Project Management Next Generation (Kerzner, Zeitoun & Vargas, 2022) — Pillar 8: Adaptive Frameworks and Life Cycles (project closure: contractual closure)
question: A fixed-price contractor has delivered and installed all equipment for a water-treatment plant expansion, and the plant has verified performance against the specifications. Before the contract is closed, the contractor submits a $48,000 claim for extra site work that it says was caused by inaccurate soil data in your bid documents. Your engineer disputes part of the claim. The procurement manager wants the contract closed this month. What should the project manager do?
options: Close the contract as scheduled, since all deliverables have been accepted and the price was fixed under the agreement
Withhold final acceptance of the equipment until the contractor agrees to withdraw its claim for the extra site work
Resolve the claim through the contract's claims procedure, preferably by negotiation, before completing contract closure
Pay the claim in full so that contract closure is not delayed and the good working relationship with the contractor is kept
hint: What must be settled before a procurement can be formally closed, and which process governs disagreements?
why: Contractual closure requires confirming that all work is complete and accepted and that all claims and disputes are settled. Even under a fixed price, the contractor may be entitled to extra payment if the buyer's own documents (here, the soil data) were inaccurate, so the claim must be evaluated on its merits. Following the contract's claims procedure — negotiation first, then mediation or arbitration only if needed — resolves it properly before the contract is closed.
how: For claims at contract closeout: evaluate them against the contract terms, settle through the agreed claims administration (negotiate first, then alternative dispute resolution), and only then formally close the procurement.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Closing with an open claim leaves a live dispute; a fixed price does not cancel entitlements arising from the buyer's own documents.
Incorrect — Holding verified work hostage to force a withdrawal is coercive, conflicts with the contract and damages trust and fairness.
Correct — Evaluating and settling the claim through the agreed procedure, starting with negotiation, must come before contractual closure.
Incorrect — Paying a partly disputed amount without evaluation wastes funds and sidesteps the buyer's duty to manage claims on their merits.
deepDive: Kerzner identifies administrative and contractual closure as the core of traditional project closure once deliverables are accepted. Contractual closure includes verifying deliverables, settling claims, finalizing payments, confirming warranties and archiving the procurement file. In PMI's claims administration, contested changes are claims; negotiation is preferred, followed by alternative dispute resolution such as mediation or arbitration. Differing site conditions caused by inaccurate buyer information are a classic source of legitimate claims even under fixed-price contracts.
